chapter_theme: Natrinai 61 to 80: night-long longing hidden from the mother, girls shut in the house and gossip pressing on secret love; men turned away who call the girl their only medicine; friends who keep the man from leaving for wealth that does not last; an evening of mullai and a shore at sunset; a mother picturing her eloped daughter's eyes; and Malaiyan's raid made the measure of a lover's lost relief.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் வரவு உணர்ந்து தலைவிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the speaker suffering through the night

61.reading: The speaker tells her friend that last night, tormented by longing and breathing hot, she suffered like a doe struck by an arrow; her mother, as if she guessed the cause, asked 'Don't you sleep, my little one?', and she, keeping the words from coming out, said softly in her heart: can eyes sleep for those who long for the man of the forest land, where by the rain-washed rock the stony hollow holds jasmine buds like a kingfisher's beak?
61.nuance: The answer is never spoken: the reply to the mother is made inside the heart (சொல் வெளிப்படாமை), so the poem shows secrecy holding even at the moment the mother comes closest to knowing. The colophon makes the friend the speaker, voicing this as the heroine's night so that the man, who has come and stands near, hears what his delay costs.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is lord of the forest land of rock and rain, and the hour is the night

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon says she speaks as if to the heroine, knowing the man has come; the poem's 'I' is the heroine's night voiced by the friend

colophon.thurai: முன் ஒரு காலத்துப்பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைவன் பின்னும் பொருள்வலிக்கப்பட்ட நெஞ்சிற்குச் செலவு அழுங்குவித்தது

comparisons.tenor: the groan of the wind-rubbed bamboos

62.reading: Pressed again toward wealth, the man reminds his heart how on the earlier journey, in the long-summer bamboo waste where wind-rubbed bamboos groan like a tethered elephant's weary sigh, he stood looking at the moon climbing the hill and thought: we too have a moon of our own, her sweet-smelling, tilakam-marked forehead, beyond that stony mountain where hot roaring wind has stripped the shade and left the trees dry.
62.nuance: The refusal to go is never stated: the poem offers only a memory, and the memory is enough. The moon he saw on the road is demoted to a second moon; the first is at home, so the journey is pictured as going away from the light.

thinai_evidence.note: long summer, shadeless dried trees: the parched road of separation

63.reading: With the man standing by, the friend says the clamorous shore town, where fishermen dry their catch on fresh sand and the punnai blooms with a festival fragrance over the stench of fish, has no justice; so the unjust mother has put the girl under strict guard, and their bond with the lord of the wave-washed shore, whose dark-winged horses rise over the flower-choked backwater mud and are washed by the sea, may waste into pallor and die.
63.nuance: The word அறன் is used twice in two lines, of the town and of the mother: gossip and guard are the same injustice seen from outside and inside the house. The bond, not the girl, is what turns pale (பசலை), a bold shift of the lovesick sign onto the relation itself.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, punnai and the lord of the shore

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடைத் தலைவியது அருமை கண்டு தூதுவிடக் கருதிய தோழிக்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது

comparisons.vehicle: சிறியிலைச் சாந்தம் வறனுற்று ஆர முருக்கி பையென மரம் வறிதாகச் சோர்ந்து உக்காங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her body emptied once her mind and heart went to him

64.reading: When her friend wants to send him word, the woman says: stop thinking of him, whatever he is; what is the friendship of one who left us like this? As the small-leaved sandal tree that the hill Kuravar, clad in maral fibre, cut without knowing dries in the drought and slowly withers to an empty trunk, so my mind and heart have gone to him and my body is empty; even if he comes he is no medicine for this sickness, so let him stay there, and let my kin not see the suffering of love that crushes me.
64.nuance: The sandal tree is cut 'without knowing' (அறியாது), so the image blames carelessness, not cruelty; that is why she can refuse him without hating him. Her last wish is not for him but that her kin should not see: secrecy outlives hope.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill Kuravar and the sandal tree

comparisons.tenor: the steep banks of the forest river

65.reading: The friend, delighted, says: may our neighbour woman eat ambrosia, for she said 'he will come', the man of the great mountain land where, at the bright ford of a white waterfall and a forest river banked like a moat with swirling moss, an elephant wounded in a fight with a tiger is beset by pitiless hunters who covet its tusk, and their fearsome clamour sounds through the thunder.
65.nuance: The neighbour's chance words are taken as an omen (the colophon's விரிச்சி): the friend blesses an unknowing speaker for a sentence not meant for them. The violent hill scene that follows is the land's ordinary life, offered as the man's address, not as a warning.

thinai_evidence.note: tiger, elephant, hill hunters and the lord of the great hill

comparisons.tenor: the sharp taste of the ukaay fruit

66.reading: The mother, at home after her daughter has left with her lover, wonders whether on the hot dusty track, where a dull dove, having pecked the pepper-sharp small fruits of the dry-topped ukaay, climbs a lonely long branch and, ruffling its spotted neck, moans, her deceitful little girl's flower-like eyes, which used to weep away their beauty if her garland was disarranged, her small bangle loosened or her coin girdle shifted, are now red, dimmed and troubled, even though she is with the man she loves.
66.nuance: The mother does not doubt the man; she grants that the girl has joined him (புணர்ந்தனள் ஆயினும்). Her worry is built from memory of tiny vanities, so the measure of the road's hardship is a childhood in which a loosened bangle was a disaster. மாயக் குறுமகள், 'deceitful little girl', is tender, not reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the ukaay, the moaning dove and the hot dusty track

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the mother muses aloud at home with no named hearer

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rising waves

iraicchi.act: the herons, having fed, settle together on the punnai for the night
iraicchi.sense: even the birds come home to roost at dusk, so the man too should stay and make this town his home, that is, marry

67.reading: As the man who came for the day meeting turns to go, the friend says the red sun has crossed the far sky and hidden behind the great hill, the ford is lonely, the black-legged white herons that fed on prawns have settled on the black-branched punnai, paired sharks prowl the backwater hiding the big flowers, and our men, lighting lamps on the cold dark sea, have gone fishing: so what harm if you stayed in our seaside town where the spray-flinging waves rise with the sound of drums?
67.nuance: The invitation to stay one night is the pressure to marry: a man who sleeps in her town must become its son-in-law. The detail that 'our men' are out on the sea makes the offer bolder than it sounds, and the prowling sharks quietly tell him the shore path is no place for a night journey.

thinai_evidence.note: sunset on the lonely shore ford

68.reading: With the man outside, the friend tells the girl: if we found someone to bow and say skilfully that for young girls to sit shut in the house, not playing orai with their companions, is neither right nor good for the household, and that they should bathe to their heart's content in the swelling new flood that carries small foam and pushes fragrant flowers, would mother let us go? Meanwhile at midnight, in half-dark, the mighty thunder roars spitting light, lightning flashes like waving banners, and the drifting cloud has settled on his high-peaked hill.
68.nuance: The friend's speech is a request for an intercessor, and the man listening is the obvious one: the person who can 'bow and speak' to the mother is a suitor asking for her. The storm on his hill at midnight closes the night path as firmly as the mother closes the door.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight storm on the hill

iraicchi.act: at evening the stag embraces his doe
iraicchi.sense: even the stag is with his mate at nightfall, which the absent husband is not

69.reading: The wife who cannot bear his absence on work says: the many-rayed sun has done its day and set behind the far high hill, birds go home to their young, in the scrub the dark-necked stag embraces his gentle doe, jasmine buds open their mouths, thondri lights up the bushes, and the clear bells of the proud cows blend with the flutes of the cowherds with crooked staves in this pitiless evening; if evening came like this in the land where he went for his work, he could not hold to his resolve.
69.nuance: She does not accuse him; she supposes that his land has no such evening, since if it had he would be home. The excuse is also a reproach, and it keeps her faith intact.

thinai_evidence.note: evening in the scrub, the jasmine, cowherds and cattle

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the friend is assumed

70.reading: The woman calls to the little white heron, whose bright feathers are like the pure folds of cloth washed at the ford: you come to our town, search our drinking ford, eat the roe-filled keliru fish and go back to his town; is it your love or your great forgetfulness that you never tell the man of that good field town, whose sweet water spreads here, of my grief and my loosening bangles?
70.nuance: The heron already travels the route a messenger would take and eats at her ford, so its silence is a kind of ingratitude; the line about water flowing from his town to hers says the towns are joined while the man is not.

thinai_evidence.note: field towns joined by fresh water, the keliru of the ford

iraicchi.act: the male dove that lives in the house calls for its mate
iraicchi.sense: a bird that stays at home calls its mate, while the man means to leave his; she will hear in it the call he will not make

71.reading: The friend tells the man bent on the sickness for wealth that does not last: if you beg her friend in many ways to tell this to the bangled girl, she may let you go, saying 'go'; but if she does, can you stand before her, stroke her eyes and forehead and leave, sir, while the red-legged male of the coloured dove living under the inner eaves of a rich house calls its beloved mate in a helpless moaning voice, and each time she hears it alone without you, the woman of thick hair will tremble?
71.nuance: The friend concedes the woman's consent in advance, then removes its value: the leave-taking itself, the hand on her eyes, is what he cannot survive. மன்னாப் பொருள் calls wealth impermanent at the poem's first word.

thinai_evidence.note: the threatened departure for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the friendship of the two women

72.reading: With the man outside, the friend tells the girl: it is shameful that the great do not cherish what they should; in a flawless friendship like one life between us, hiding anything from you would be a great wrong; once, when I said I feared mother, the lord of the shore would never think of leaving; now, even though our shore companions may know, he keeps asking 'has gossip come?', so I fear in my heart, friend, that his friendship is drying up.
72.nuance: The man's new question about gossip is read as a sign of cooling: caution once came from the girl's side and now comes from his. The friend speaks it within the women's own friendship (உயிர் ஓரன்ன) so the listener feels judged by two.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and its lord

colophon.thurai: செலவுக் குறிப்பு அறிந்து வேறுபட்ட தலைவி சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the long bent ears of red rice

73.reading: The woman says that they say he will leave us here, we who are afraid even with him, in the cruel evening when the strong-mouthed ghoul with ungainly fingers like the ripe clusters of the summer murukku splits the public square to eat the flower offerings of the rich old town; pitiable then are the pallor that ruins my forehead, once lovely as Saykkadu with its flowered gardens where the swan sleeps in red-rice fields whose long bent ears are like rows of red hair, and the gossip the neighbours spread.
73.nuance: The fear is set at home, not on his road: it is the town's evening, with its ghoul in the square, that she will face alone. Her past beauty is measured by a rich field town, so what the pallor destroys is a kind of wealth, the very thing he leaves to seek.

thinai_evidence.note: his coming departure, leaving her behind

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee and the stage are not given; the neighbours' gossip may mean the parting before marriage

comparisons.tenor: the fishermen pushing the laden boat

ullurai.tenor: the woman whom the town now knows as the man's

pairs.situation: the town's talk, gust after gust
the name of his woman heaped on her until it cannot be brushed off

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the punnai and herons of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

74.reading: Refusing the bard who comes for the man, the woman says they call even the lord of the great shore of small-flowered nyazhal, where fishermen push the boat loaded with a great net of strong twisted cord into the thunder-voiced sea as elephant-keepers with goads drive an elephant hard to hold, a stranger now; yet the town knows me as the woman of him whose town has kandal hedges by the clear sea, where each gust of the east wind shakes the fine pollen of the punnai in the fresh-sand grove until it heaps on the white backs of the herons, and that is hard to undo.
74.nuance: She refuses entry while admitting she cannot undo the bond: the town's knowledge makes her his whether he behaves or not. The punnai's pollen settling on the herons' backs is the image of a mark that the wind keeps adding and nothing washes off.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, nyazhal, punnai and kandal of the shore

75.reading: Turned away, the man says to the girl, so that her friend hears: not thinking 'this is the fruit of unkindness', as one might torment the life of a snake with a fire-spitting broad hood of bright spots, this is not fitting here; long live, little one: speak without laughing, for my heart is breaking; tell me how my aching heart can live, struck by the glance that will not look of your large rain-cool eyes streaked with red, like the arrow wet with raw flesh that the hill hunter with curved bow shot to kill a tusked beast on the slope.
75.nuance: உறாஅ நோக்கம், the look that does not touch, is the weapon: indifference wounds like a hunter's arrow. Asking her to speak 'without laughing' shows he fears her mockery more than her refusal.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter and the tusked beast on the hill slope

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks to the girl (குறுமகள்) so that the friend, who has kept him off, may hear

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்து உடன்போகாநின்ற தலைவன் இடைச் சுரத்துத் தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது அம்மூவனார்

76.reading: Eloping with her, the man tells the girl on the way: in this forest of dry trees under a white sky that has hidden the coming rain and stopped even fine drizzle, rest from weariness in the banyan's shade; unafraid where there is cause for fear, resting where it is right to rest, go on without strain, girl of bright jewels, so that your soft feet, used to the long sand of the shore grove of your town, where the great gossip hums and fallen punnai flowers smell of honey and fish, and now reddened against the stones, may recover.
76.nuance: Her old town is remembered for its gossip and its soft sand in one breath: what she has left is both what hurt her and what was gentle to her feet. He sets the pace by her feet, not by the road.

thinai_evidence.note: a rainless forest of dried trees on the elopement road

occasion.words: உடன்போகாநின்ற தலைவன் இடைச் சுரத்துத் தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது

comparisons.tenor: the relief her look once gave him

77.reading: The man who keeps following her tells his heart: as Malaiyan rode his horse into enemy land with the Pulaiyan's great tudi drum sounding, broke their hard strongholds and then breathed out his weariness, so once, heart, the glad innocent look of her kuvalai-dark kohl eyes brought me relief: the bright-browed girl with spotted hips, whose forearm is filled with broad bangles that the skilled smith of the small town of Ooral filed with a saw, where in the yard full of jackfruit hanging on every branch, the housewife sleeps at night to the roar of the white waterfall.
77.nuance: மன்னே marks the relief as past: the poem is spoken now that it is gone. The king's sigh comes after the raid, not during it, so the comparison is to exhausted ease after victory, not to conquest; the woman of the yard who sleeps by the waterfall's noise is the calm he no longer has.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit yard and the waterfall of a hill hamlet

78.reading: The friend tells the girl: in the shore grove fragrant with the hanging-rooted thazhai, where in the dark backwater gleaming like a sword and roamed by killing sharks the punnai sprinkles fine gold-like pollen to fill the great gem-blue neythal flowers, we shall now escape the grief that torments us at the evening hour when the sun goes; listen, friend: the bell of the chariot of the lord of the mighty sea, whose horses with golden trappings leap like rising birds so that the charioteer never has to touch them with the whip, even when the sharp wheel-rims sink into the clear backwater.
78.nuance: The chariot is heard, not seen: the bell's sound alone is news of marriage. The horses that need no whip carry the point that he now comes of his own eagerness, not pressed.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal, punnai, thazhai and sharks of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the friend is the usual bearer of this news, and she calls the girl தோழி

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்ந்து வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the eengai flowers fallen on the rock

79.reading: Sensing he will leave, the woman tells her friend: shall we tell him our love, saying 'is anything harder than this, that those who parted come back and join us and then, having joined, plan to part again, by the forked path hard to cross where clustered eengai flowers fall on the rock like the molucca seeds that bangled girls of good houses play with on sand?' If we don't tell him, it has come for life itself; so, friend, by what can we stop the lover's going?
79.nuance: The argument she rehearses is a small piece of logic about cycles: union after parting should make parting harder, not easier. The last line asks for a means, not a reason: she already knows words may not be enough.

thinai_evidence.note: his planned departure

colophon.thurai: சேட்படுக்கப்பட்டு ஆற்றானாய தலைவன் தோழி கேட்ப தன் நெஞ்சிற்கு உரைத்தது

80.reading: Kept away, the man tells his heart so the friend can hear: in the dawn when the town's small boys, wanting the sweet milk of the common's dark buffalo with flowering head, loose its calf and ride it off, she came eager, and with her jewelled companions, restrained by fitting shyness and saying 'this one brought leaf skirts and garlands', she bathes in the cool pond in the month of Thai; there is no medicine but that broad-shouldered girl for the sickness I have.
80.nuance: His gifts (தழையும் தாரும்) are named in her voice, so he knows she has noticed him; the friend's refusal is answered by her own acknowledgement. The Thai bath is a maidens' rite, which makes her not yet anyone's.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover's suit before marriage, his gifts and his sickness: the situation of kurinji

links.note: In Natrinai 80 the man says there is no medicine but the girl for his sickness; in Natrinai 64 the deserted woman says that even if he comes he is no medicine for her sickness.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems show the anthology using one figure, the beloved as the only cure, at both ends of secret love: the pursuing man asserts it and the abandoned woman revokes it, so the claim holds only while hope does.

links.note: Both have the man say that the woman herself is the only cure for the sickness she causes; the Kural states it as a paradox of medicine, Natrinai 80 says it to his own heart so that the friend who keeps him off will hear.
links.teaches: The couplet's general paradox becomes in the older poem a lever in a negotiation: by declaring the girl his only medicine where her guardian can overhear, the rejected man turns a private conceit into a claim on the friend's pity.

links.note: In both the woman tells her friend that the man's departure must be stopped because union after he goes will be hard; Natrinai 79 rehearses the words she might say and asks by what means to stop him.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the friend a reason to act, while the Natrinai woman supplies the argument she would use, that rejoining after parting makes another parting harder, and then doubts any words will work; the poem shows the couplet's advice as a thing she has already tried in her head.

links.note: Both are the friend's speech to a man about to leave: Kural 1151 says tell me only if you are not going, and tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 71 grants the woman may let him go and asks whether he can stroke her eyes and leave.
links.teaches: The couplet argues from the woman's death, the Natrinai friend from the man's own tenderness at the moment of leave-taking, so the two show the dissuasion speech had two separate levers, her survival and his ability to bear the parting.

links.note: Natrinai 71 opens by calling wealth impermanent (மன்னாப் பொருள்) to keep the man at home; Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should do at once what lasts.
links.teaches: The same premise, that wealth does not last, yields opposite advice: the Kural tells a man to seek and spend it on what endures, the friend uses it to argue he should not seek it at all, which shows nilaiyaamai served the akam poets as a rhetorical weapon before it was a doctrine.

links.note: Both are the friend speaking to the woman while the man overhears, about the town's gossip; in Kural 1150 the gossip is welcome because it will push him to marry, in Natrinai 72 his anxiety about gossip is read as a sign his love is drying up.
links.teaches: In the same speech situation the friend can treat gossip as an ally or as a threat depending on how the man reacts to it, so the pair shows that alar works on the lover's resolve, not on the woman's name.

links.note: Both concern the woman's indifferent glance in early love: Kural 1099 says looking at each other like strangers is found only in lovers; in Natrinai 75 the rejected man says her glance that does not look has wounded him like a hunter's arrow.
links.teaches: The look the Kural's observer reads as proof of love is, to the man who receives it, a fatal wound, so the pair shows the same sign read from outside as a disguise and from inside as a refusal.

links.note: Both have the wife alone at evening hearing the cowherds' flutes; Kural 1228 calls the flute the messenger of evening and a killing weapon, Natrinai 69 sets the flutes and cow bells among the evening's signs and says that if such an evening came where he is, he could not stay at his work.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the evening's music a weapon only against her, while the Natrinai wife imagines it falling on him too and so excuses his absence by supposing his land has no such evenings, turning the same lament into a defence of his love.

links.note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is, since their own steadfastness is the best guard; in Natrinai 68 the friend says shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for the household.
links.teaches: Both reject confinement, but the Kural does so for the wife because her virtue makes it needless, while the Natrinai girls reject it for the unmarried daughter because it blocks a love headed for marriage, so the same verdict rests on opposite views of what the woman's will is for.

links.note: Purananuru 158 lists Malaiyan who rode Kaari and won great battles among the seven givers; in Natrinai 77 Kapilar likens the relief the girl's look once gave the lover to Malaiyan riding his horse into enemy land, breaking forts and breathing out his weariness.
links.teaches: The puram poem keeps Malaiyan as a rider and giver in a public roll, while the akam poem takes the same rider at the private moment after the raid, his sigh of relief, so akam used the king's fame for the feeling of a finished deed rather than for the deed.

source_issues: 66, 70, 76, 77, 78: the colophon thurai ends with the poet's name (இனிசந்த நாகனார், வெள்ளி வீதியார், அம்மூவனார், கபிலர், கீரங்கீரனார}) and the poet field is empty; copied as printed.
61: the colophon makes the friend the speaker, but the poem's 'I' lies awake and is asked by her mother why she does not sleep; read as the friend voicing the heroine's night.
65: line 7 விற் சுழிப்பட்ட is obscure; the hunters' clamour and the thunder in line 8 may be compared or merely heard together.
75: lines 1 to 3 (பாம்பு உயிர் அணங்கியாங்கும்) are hard to construe; the reading takes them as a comparison for cruelty.
79: line 1 சிறை நாள் is obscure; the season of the eengai bloom is not fixed.
78: the colophon names no speaker; the friend is assumed.
80: line 9 is repeated in Natrinai 140 line 11 (text flag).
